meta.titre: ATR Death and the Afterlife at Advanced Level: causes of death, funeral rites and the ancestors
meta.sous_theme: Beliefs about the causes of death, the funeral rites and the life after death in ATR
tags: A Level Religious Studies - atr death and the afterlife

source.epreuve_titre: GCE A/L Religious Studies past paper (Cameroon)

sections.contenu_markdown: In Cameroon a funeral is rarely a small family event. Relatives travel from the cities, neighbours bring food and help, and the ceremonies may continue for several days. This scale shows how seriously many communities take death. In African Traditional Religion (ATR) death is understood as an important change in a person's existence, and the way a person dies and is buried is believed to affect both the dead and the living. Examiners ask why people die, what happens afterwards and why the rites matter, so you need to answer with belief, practice and reasoning, and you must show that customs vary from people to people.

items: Many African peoples believe that God created human beings and set the length of life.
Ancestors are deceased members of a family or community who are remembered and honoured by their descendants.
A rite is a set form of words and actions performed for religious or social purposes.

sections.titre: Death, burial rites and the hereafter in ATR
sections.contenu_markdown:
### Death as a passage
In ATR, death is generally seen as a passage from the visible world to the spiritual world and not as the end of existence. The dead person is believed to continue to exist and to remain linked with the family. Practices differ widely, so introduce your points with 'in many communities'.

### Causes of death as explained in ATR
| Explanation | What adherents believe |
|---|---|
| God's will | God gives life and fixes its limit; death in old age is accepted as the end of a full life. |
| Displeasure of the ancestors or spirits | Neglect of duties or the breaking of a taboo may lead them to withdraw protection or allow sickness. |
| Witchcraft and sorcery | Many believe that a person with harmful mystical power can cause illness and early death, so a diviner may be consulted. |
| Curses, broken oaths and serious offences | Wrongdoing, especially against kin or the community, is thought to bring death as a consequence. |
| Natural causes | Sickness, accident and age are recognised as physical causes, but people also ask why this person died at this time, and the answer is often sought in the spiritual world. |

Many communities distinguish a 'good death', usually in old age at home after raising a family, from a 'bad death', for example the death of a young person, a death by accident or the death of a person without children. A bad death may call for special rites.

### Funeral rites and their importance
Rites vary, but often include announcing the death, washing and dressing the body, mourning, burial, a communal meal, libation and prayer to the ancestors, and in some communities a later memorial ceremony. Their importance:
- They help the dead person to join the ancestors, so that the person is not left unsettled.
- They honour the dead and express family duty and love.
- They comfort the bereaved and gather the community, which strengthens solidarity.
- They restore order, may settle questions of inheritance and succession and mark the end of mourning.
- They keep good relations with the ancestors, who are believed to protect the living if properly honoured.

### The hereafter
The next life is usually described as life in the spiritual world, close to the living and similar to this life. John Mbiti called ancestors who are still remembered by name the 'living-dead'. They receive libations, watch over the family and are believed to act as intermediaries to God. Many communities do not speak of a final judgement in the way other religions do, and some peoples believe that ancestors may be reborn in a new child of the family.

variantes.nom: Question on the causes of death
variantes.quand_utiliser: When asked what causes death, why people die or how death is explained.
variantes.contenu_markdown: Give four or five explanations from the table, and for each state the belief and the reaction, for example consulting a diviner. Make clear that physical causes are also recognised, and that the stress on spiritual causes answers the question 'why?'.

variantes.nom: Question on funeral rites or the hereafter
variantes.quand_utiliser: When asked about the importance of death rituals, or to explain the idea of the hereafter.
variantes.contenu_markdown: For rites, name the main rites and attach a purpose to each. For the hereafter, explain the idea of continued existence in the spiritual world, the role of the living-dead and the link between proper burial and a peaceful passage. State that details differ among peoples.

sections.enonce_markdown: Explain why the manner of a person's death matters in African Traditional Religion. (12 marks)

etapes.justification: 'Explain why' asks for reasons, and 'manner of death' points to the difference between good and bad death.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Plan: introduction on death as a passage; good death; bad death; consequences for rites and the living; conclusion.

etapes.justification: The belief about death as a passage gives the reason for the importance of how it happens.
etapes.resultat_markdown: In many communities death is a passage to the spiritual world, and it is believed that the way a person dies affects that passage.

etapes.justification: A contrast makes the answer clear.
etapes.resultat_markdown: A death in old age, at home, after a full life with children is usually seen as complete and the person is expected to join the ancestors.

etapes.action: Describe a bad death and its consequences.
etapes.justification: Consequences show why the manner matters.
etapes.resultat_markdown: The death of a young person, a death by accident or the death of a person without children is often seen as untimely. It may call for special rites, and diviners may be asked for the cause.

etapes.action: Show the effect on the living and conclude.
etapes.justification: A final link to the community and to the ancestors completes the explanation.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Correct rites protect the family from fear of an unsettled spirit and keep good relations with the ancestors, so the manner of death matters for the dead and for the living.

sections.conclusion_markdown: **Model answer (key points).** In many African communities death is not the end of existence but a passage to the spiritual world, and the manner of a person's death is believed to affect that passage. A death in old age, after a full life and with descendants, is regarded as good: the person is expected to join the ancestors and to be remembered as one of the living-dead. A death that comes early, by accident or without children is often seen as untimely and may be linked by diviners to spiritual causes. Such a death can call for special rites so that the dead person is settled and the family protected. The manner of death therefore matters for the dead person, for the family and for the relations between the living and the ancestors.

items.erreur_markdown: Writing that ATR has no belief in life after death.
items.pourquoi_faux: In ATR death is generally seen as a passage, and the dead are believed to continue to exist in the spiritual world and to remain linked with the family.
items.correction_markdown: Explain the belief in the spiritual world and the role of the living-dead.

items.erreur_markdown: Saying that death is explained only by spiritual causes, as if Africans ignore sickness and accidents.
items.pourquoi_faux: Physical causes are recognised. The spiritual explanation answers the further question of why this person died at this time.
items.correction_markdown: Write that physical causes are accepted, while the spiritual explanation seeks the deeper reason.

items.erreur_markdown: Using the words 'heaven' and 'hell' as the standard ATR belief.
items.pourquoi_faux: Many communities do not describe the next life as a place of reward and punishment as in other religions. Mixing the vocabulary of other religions distorts the belief.
items.correction_markdown: Describe the hereafter as the spiritual world and the community of ancestors, and note that details vary.

items.erreur_markdown: Listing funeral practices without saying why they are performed.
items.pourquoi_faux: A question on importance asks for purpose. A list of actions earns few marks.
items.correction_markdown: Attach a reason to each rite, such as helping the dead to join the ancestors, honouring the dead, comforting the bereaved or restoring order.

items.erreur_markdown: Presenting the funeral customs of one people as if they applied everywhere.
items.pourquoi_faux: Customs differ greatly, and the generalisation is inaccurate.
items.correction_markdown: Use 'in many communities' or 'among some peoples' when giving examples.

items.enonce_markdown: State three explanations for death found in ATR. (3 marks)
items.solution_markdown: Award one mark for each explanation named, for example God's will, the anger of the ancestors or spirits, witchcraft or sorcery, a curse or breach of a taboo. **Three explanations, one mark each.**

items.enonce_markdown: Explain two reasons why the funeral of an elderly person is often a major community event in ATR. (6 marks)
items.solution_markdown: Award marks for any two developed reasons, 3 marks each: an elderly person's death is regarded as the end of a full life and a good death, so it is honoured with a large ceremony and a communal meal (3 marks); the funeral helps the dead person to join the ancestors and keeps good relations with them, so the community takes care to perform the rites well (3 marks); the funeral gathers relatives and neighbours, comforts the bereaved and strengthens solidarity (3 marks); the funeral may settle inheritance and succession (3 marks). **Two developed reasons.**

items.enonce_markdown: Evaluate the claim that ancestors are 'living-dead' and not dead in the full sense. (20 marks)
items.solution_markdown: Plan and marking points. Introduction: ancestors defined and the term 'living-dead' linked with Mbiti (3 marks). In support: the dead are believed to continue to exist in the spiritual world near the family, are remembered by name, receive libations, watch over the family and act as intermediaries to God, and in some views are reborn in a descendant (up to 8 marks). Against or limits: a person who dies without proper rites or a bad death may not become an ancestor, memory of an ancestor fades after some generations, and the dead cannot take part in the physical life of the community as the living do (up to 6 marks). Conclusion: a judgement that, within ATR, ancestors are regarded as still present and active, though in a different mode of existence (3 marks). **Credit a reasoned judgement supported by examples.**

items_markdown: In ATR, death is generally seen as a passage to the spiritual world and not as the end of a person.
Causes of death are explained by God's will, the displeasure of ancestors or spirits, witchcraft or sorcery, curses and broken taboos, as well as by physical causes.
A good death (old age, a full life) differs from a bad death (untimely, accidental or childless); a bad death may require special rites.
Funeral rites help the dead to join the ancestors, honour the dead, comfort the bereaved, strengthen the community and restore order.
Ancestors who are remembered are the 'living-dead'; they are believed to protect the family and to act as intermediaries.
Customs differ among peoples: use 'in many communities' and avoid the vocabulary of other religions.
